part_title: What Cloud Computing Is and Why Businesses Use It
review_basis: Individually inspected AIF Module 02 original WebPs 07–13: cloud access, request-response security, everyday services, deployment types, essential characteristics and matched benefits.

scenes.title: What is cloud computing?
scenes.narration: Start with the student on the left requesting a computing resource using a laptop. In traditional IT, a company might buy a physical server, install it, and wait for its IT team to configure it. Cloud computing changes how we obtain that resource. The central picture shows AWS operating buildings full of servers, networking equipment and storage. AWS maintains the underlying infrastructure, and the customer requests services when needed. The arrow from the laptop toward the cloud is labeled request resources. The arrow moving right shows the result: compute power, data storage, applications and other IT services. Compute means processing power that runs programs. Storage means retaining files or records. An API, which stands for application programming interface, is another way for software to request a service automatically instead of someone clicking through the web console. Look at the four boxes underneath. On demand means getting resources without purchasing hardware first. Right sizing means choosing an appropriate size, rather than always choosing the biggest server. Scaling means increasing or reducing resources when demand changes. Pay as you go means cloud charges are commonly linked to consumption, although some resources have minimum charges or commitments. Imagine a graduate starting an online shop. At first, a small server may be enough. During a promotion, the shop may need more capacity. Instead of buying a room full of machines in advance, the team can adjust its cloud resources. But cloud is not automatically free or cheap: an unused running server can still generate charges. Quick check: does cloud computing mean AWS writes and secures your whole application for you? No. AWS provides infrastructure and managed services, while customers retain responsibilities for their applications and data.

scenes.title: Accessing cloud resources over a network
scenes.narration: Trace the diagram from the laptop on the left, through the globe in the center, and into the AWS cloud on the right. Your laptop is the client, which means it asks for something. The globe represents the network, usually the internet, connecting your device to the provider. AWS provides different destinations: computing services to run applications, storage to hold information, and AI services to add capabilities such as text analysis. The blue arrow moving right is the request. The yellow arrow returning left is the response. Consider a university student submitting a project file. Their browser sends a request to an application running on cloud infrastructure, the application stores the document, and the server sends back a confirmation. Now look at the four numbered steps along the bottom. First, connect to a network. Second, send a request, perhaps through a browser or an API. Third, receive the result. Fourth, use secure access. Encryption is a way to transform information so unauthorized observers cannot easily read it while it travels. HTTPS is a common encrypted web connection. However, encryption in transit is only one layer. The application must also authenticate the user, which means verifying who they are, and authorize access, which means deciding what they are permitted to do. A network connection does not automatically grant permission to every AWS resource. Some AWS services can also be reached over private connectivity instead of the public internet. A small decision question: if a student can open a university website but cannot see another student's grades, which control is important besides networking? Authorization, because access to data must be restricted to the right person.

scenes.title: Cloud services in everyday life
scenes.narration: Cloud computing is already part of familiar everyday experiences. Look at the three large panels across this slide. On the left is cloud email. You can open the same mailbox on a phone and laptop because the messages are stored and synchronized through an online service. Synchronization means changes, such as reading or moving an email, can be reflected across devices. In the middle is cloud file storage. A student could upload a project document and share it with a teammate, who opens it from another location. Sharing permissions still matter: uploading a file does not mean everyone should see it. On the right is video streaming. A video service delivers content to different screens and may use servers and caching systems positioned closer to viewers. These examples are different applications but share the same foundation. At the bottom, follow the request arrow from the laptop through the network to the cloud provider, and the response arrow returning from the provider. The customer uses the application without personally managing its underlying servers. That does not mean every cloud service belongs to AWS; cloud computing is an industry-wide approach used by many providers. Consider your college submitting online assignments. If your learning portal remains available from home and university, it may use cloud-hosted application and storage services, though a similar service could also be hosted elsewhere. What is the main advantage for the student? Access to the service through a network without owning the server. And what is one responsibility that remains? Protecting your account and understanding who can access your uploaded work.

scenes.title: Public, private and hybrid cloud
scenes.narration: The slide compares three ways to deploy cloud-style computing. Start on the left with public cloud. A provider such as AWS offers computing resources to many customers on a shared physical infrastructure, while isolating each customer's data and workload through technical security controls. Shared infrastructure does not mean that other customers automatically see your files. In the center is private cloud, a dedicated cloud environment intended for one organization. The organization may choose this for particular control, governance, customization or compliance requirements, although private does not automatically mean safer. Strong security still depends on configuration and operation. On the right is hybrid cloud. This connects private environments with public cloud services so an organization can use both. Follow the glowing connection between the two environments. The retailer example at the bottom gives a concrete reason: a company might keep a sensitive legacy payment-related system in a controlled private environment while placing its public website and seasonal processing capacity in the public cloud. Whether that design satisfies payment rules depends on its actual security architecture, not simply calling the system private. Hybrid arrangements also introduce integration, identity, networking and monitoring challenges. Here is a decision practice question. A college runs a legacy laboratory system it cannot immediately move, but it wants to add a public cloud application for students. Which deployment approach could connect the two? A hybrid architecture. However, if there is no special need for a private environment, a public cloud deployment may be simpler. Choose the deployment model from actual business and technical constraints, not just the name.

scenes.title: The five characteristics of cloud computing
scenes.narration: These five columns explain what makes cloud computing different from simply renting a fixed server. Column one is on-demand self-service. The laptop with a Launch button represents requesting resources directly when needed, without waiting for a provider employee to approve each action. Column two is broad network access. The laptop, phone and tablet show that a service can be accessed through standard network mechanisms from different suitable devices. Column three illustrates resource pooling. The provider uses shared capacity to serve multiple customers, with isolation between their workloads. Multi-tenancy is a related term meaning a service or infrastructure can host separate customers, called tenants. Customers must not be able to read each other's private information just because the hardware is shared. Column four shows rapid elasticity. The bars grow and shrink, meaning capacity can adjust as demand changes. Elasticity is more specific than growth: it includes reducing capacity when it is no longer required. Column five is measured service. The invoice and gauge indicate that usage can be monitored and associated with charges, though actual billing differs by service. The online store along the bottom ties everything together. Customers shop from multiple devices, the store uses shared provider capacity, more resources can be added for holiday demand and usage is measured. Notice an important distinction: scalability is the ability to support larger or smaller workloads, while elasticity emphasizes adjusting capacity to actual demand. Quick check: an online store doubles its resources for a sale and releases the extra resources afterwards. Which characteristic is especially visible? Rapid elasticity. And if the owner can create resources in the console immediately, that illustrates on-demand self-service.

scenes.title: Six advantages of cloud computing
scenes.narration: This slide presents six potential business advantages. Begin with lower upfront costs. Rather than purchasing many servers before knowing whether a new application succeeds, an organization can use cloud services and pay according to the chosen pricing model. The CAPEX label means capital expenditure, such as buying physical equipment. OPEX means operating expenditure, such as ongoing service bills. It is an accounting distinction, not a promise that cloud always costs less. Second, the provider handles much of the physical data center operation, including facilities and underlying hardware. Customers still manage the responsibilities that belong to them. Third, economies of scale means large providers may operate infrastructure efficiently because they serve many customers. This can create cost advantages, but your final bill depends on your design and consumption. Fourth, scale with demand. The upward and downward bar illustration shows adjusting capacity rather than guessing years of future need. Fifth, speed and agility: developers can experiment and launch resources faster. Agility means the ability to respond to changes without long procurement delays. Sixth, global reach: AWS provides infrastructure in multiple geographical areas, enabling deployment closer to users when supported services are available. Look at the example at the bottom. A student team launching a new application can try a small cloud environment, evaluate demand, and expand if the idea succeeds. But a running resource may continue to bill when no student is using the application, and global deployment adds data transfer and operational complexity. So the decision cue is not 'cloud is always cheapest.' Instead ask whether faster experimentation, flexible capacity and reduced physical infrastructure burden justify the costs. A quick exam-style check: which advantage best addresses waiting months for new servers? Increased speed and agility.

scenes.title: Match cloud benefits to business needs
scenes.narration: Now we must choose the right benefit for the situation. This dense slide has six columns, so follow them in order. First is flexibility: change the resource type when your workload changes. The example upgrades from a general-purpose instance to a memory-optimized instance for a heavy product-catalog job. An instance is a virtual computer running in the cloud. Second is cost effectiveness: choose suitable resources, monitor usage and avoid paying for unnecessary capacity. Third is scalability, meaning the system can handle more work. The purple diagrams compare vertical scaling, making one machine larger, with horizontal scaling, adding more machines. The example moves from one instance to three instances behind a load balancer. A load balancer distributes requests across healthy application servers. Fourth is elasticity. Notice the graph with demand rising for a flash sale and falling again. An elastic system automatically adds capacity during busy periods and removes extra capacity when demand drops. A system can be scalable without automatically scaling back down, so these terms are related but not identical. Fifth is high availability and fault tolerance. The picture shows an application spread across two Availability Zones, which are separate infrastructure locations within an AWS Region. If one location has a problem, correctly designed services in the other may continue serving users. This requires compatible application and database design; just creating two servers is not enough. Sixth is agility, represented by build, test and launch. A company can experiment with a recommendation system and release a new feature quickly. The takeaway is that AWS gives you capabilities, but architecture decisions determine actual outcomes. Let's test three cases. A retailer needs more servers only during holiday sales: elasticity. The retailer needs to survive one zone failing: high availability and fault tolerance. The retailer wants to try a prototype this afternoon: agility. Matching requirements to benefits is more useful than memorizing six words.
